extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political science, statesmen, and scholars interested in constitutional design and federalism
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition of the structure, powers, and practical effects of the Federal (U.S.) Constitution, focusing on the balance between national and state authority, separation of powers, and the strengths/weaknesses of executive and legislative design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated federal powers vs. state residual authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The attributes of the Federal Government were therefore carefully enumerated and all that was not included amongst them was declared to constitute a part of the privileges of the several Governments of the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal powers should be explicitly listed; anything not enumerated remains within state competence. This principle preserves state rule as the norm and national authority as the exception. (Surrounding discussion contrasts simple, definable federal obligations with the States' complex and various obligations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: States may legislate in areas not exclusively reserved to Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the exclusive right of regulating certain matters is not reserved to Congress by the Constitution, the States may take up the affair until it is brought before the National Assembly. For instance, Congress has the right of making a general law on bankruptcy, which, however, it neglects to do. Each State is then at liberty to make a law for itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, absent national legislation, states may fill regulatory gaps (example: bankruptcy). This allocation has been established by court discussion and belongs to jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of a high federal court to maintain balance
rubrics_metrics.description: A high Federal court was created ... which was destined, amongst other functions, to maintain the balance of power which had been established by the Constitution between the two rival Governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid submitting interstate federal-state boundary questions to ordinary state courts (which might be partial), a supreme federal tribunal resolves disputes and maintains the constitutional balance; its action is described as indirect in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal prerogatives: external relations and war/peace powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusive right of making peace and war, of concluding treaties of commerce, of raising armies, and equipping fleets, was granted to the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External sovereignty functions (war, diplomacy, treaties, armed forces) are centralized; these are compared to private individuals needing a single head to maintain external relations advantageously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal control of national infrastructure and economic policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union was invested with the power of controlling the monetary system, of directing the post office, and of opening the great roads which were to establish a communication between the different parts of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain internal interests (monetary system, postal service, national roads) are best served by general authority and thus vested in the Union; similar privileges include bankruptcy, patents, and matters requiring national intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited federal interference in internal state affairs (predetermined cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Government was authorized to interfere in the internal affairs of the States in a few predetermined cases, in which an indiscreet abuse of their independence might compromise the security of the Union at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal interference is narrow and defined, intended to prevent state actions that would threaten the Union (examples: prohibition of ex post facto laws and creation of nobility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal taxing power necessary to fulfill national engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: As it was necessary that the Federal Government should be able to fulfil its engagements, it was endowed with an unlimited power of levying taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ensure the Union can meet obligations, fiscal authority is broad at the federal level (cited constitutional sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral legislature reflecting state independence and national sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of the independence of the States prevailed in the formation of the Senate, and that of the sovereignty of the nation predominated in the composition of the House of Representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A compromise: Senate represents states equally (two senators each), House represents population proportionally. This combination blends two theoretically incompatible systems to balance small-state and popular majoritarian interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment and representation mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: It was decided that each State should send two senators to Congress, and a number of representatives proportioned to its population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apportionment is periodically adjusted by Congress (historical examples of ratios provided); the design can lead to small states' Senate equality conflicting with populous-state advantages in the House, potentially allowing senate minority to delay majority decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different modes, terms, and functions of the two Houses
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Representatives is named by the people, the Senate by the legislators of each State; the former is directly elected, the latter is elected by an elected body; the term for which the representatives are chosen is only two years, that of the senators is six.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional differences: House is primarily legislative (short term, popular), Senate co-operates in legislation, tries political offences (impeachments), ratifies treaties and confirms appointments, and acts as an executive council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive designed to be elective, responsible, and independent in its sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The American legislators undertook a difficult task in attempting to create an executive power dependent on the majority of the people, and nevertheless sufficiently strong to act without restraint in its own sphere... The President is an elective magistrate. His honor, his property, his liberty, and his life are the securities which the people has for the temperate use of his power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive should be accountable to the people yet have sufficient stability and strength (4-year term, eligible for re-election) to fulfill duties; the Constitution avoids making him subordinate to a council to preserve responsibility and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate oversight limits but does not direct the President
rubrics_metrics.description: He is free to act in his own sphere under the inspection, but not under the direction, of the Senate... The Senate has the right of annulling certain acts of the President; but it cannot compel him to take any steps, nor does it participate in the exercise of the executive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senate's role is supervisory (ratify treaties, approve appointments, try impeachments) but cannot command executive actions; dependence arises indirectly (e.g., control of salaries) and the suspensive veto and fixed salary preserve executive independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspensive veto as executive check and appeal to the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is ... provided with a suspensive veto, which allows him to oppose the passing of such laws as might destroy the portion of independence which the Constitution awards him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Veto forces legislature to reconsider and requires two-thirds majority to override; described as an appeal to the people and a means for the executive to plead its cause when legislature persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast between limited elective executive and constitutional monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive power is as limited and partial as the sovereignty of the Union; the King of France exercises a portion of the sovereign power and contributes to the nomination of the legislature... The President is merely the agent of the sovereign power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison highlights differences in duration, appointment powers, dissolution, and practical influence—monarchs may share legislative formation and have longer/durable authority, giving more effective power than an elective president.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability and scope of executive authority affect real power
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration is one of the chief elements of strength; nothing is either loved or feared but what is likely to endure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hereditary or long-duration executive roles produce sustained influence; elective, short-tenured executives are inherently weaker even if formal prerogatives appear large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances (accidental causes) can increase executive influence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the existence of the Union were perpetually threatened, ... the executive government would assume an increased importance in proportion to the measures expected of it... The President of the United States is in the possession of almost royal prerogatives, which he has no opportunity of exercising; and those privileges which he can at present use are very circumscribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External threats, size of military/fleet, and international position can magnify executive power beyond constitutional design; legal powers may be constrained by circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature can function without presidential majority due to limited executive autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Several Presidents of the United States have been known to lose the majority in the legislative body without being obliged to abandon the supreme power, and without inflicting a serious evil upon society... this is a proof of [executive] extreme weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the executive cannot prevent laws or avoid enforcing them, losing legislative support does not paralyze governance as it might in systems where the executive executes much of sovereign power; this trait indicates a weak executive rather than strong independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of electing a powerful chief magistrate increase with the extent of prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: The dangers of the system of election applied to the head of the executive government of a great people ... increase in the exact ratio of the influence exercised by the executive power in the affairs of State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elective systems can inflame private ambition and faction when the office offers great prerogatives; to make elective leadership safe, the executive sphere must be circumscribed and the populace accustomed to governing without strong executive protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical necessity of compromise in constitutional design
rubrics_metrics.description: A middle course was hit upon by the legislators, which brought together by force two systems theoretically irreconcilable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conflicting interests (state independence vs national sovereignty) exist during constitution formation, compromises (e.g., bicameralism with differing principles) are inevitable; pure logic is rarely sustained beyond early nation stages.
